allNodeData.name: Conditional Probability
allNodeData.description: $p(B|A)$ is the probability of event B, given that some other event A has occurred.

allNodeData.name: Joint Probability
allNodeData.description: $p(A AND B)$ or $p(AB)$ is the probability that both A and B will occur

allNodeData.name: Baye's Rule
allNodeData.description: If outcomes $A$ and $B$ occur with probabilities $p(A)$ and $p(B)$, the joint probability of events $A$ and $B$ is $p(AB)=P(B|A)p(A)=p(A|B)p(B)$

allNodeData.name: Degree of Correlation
allNodeData.description: The degree of correlation $g$ between events $A$ and $B$ can be expressed as the ratio of the conditional probability of $B$, given $A$, to the unconditional probability of $B$ alone: $g=\frac{p(B|A)}{p(B)}=\frac{p(AB)}{p(A)p(B)}$

allNodeData.name: Adding Joint Probabilities
allNodeData.description: $p(B) = p(BA) + p(BA') = p(B|A)p(A)+p(B|A')p(A')$. Essentially you sum the probability of $B$ occuring given all other mutually exclusive outcomes

allNodeData.name: Ordered Exclusive Events
allNodeData.description: $p(i \ is \ first | j \ is \ second | k \ is \ third)=\frac{p(i)p(j)p(k)}{[1-p(i)][1-p(i)-p(j)]}$. This follow from the fact that, once event $i$ occurs, (and is thus unable to occur again), the remaining probabilities become $\frac{p(j)}{p(j)+p(k)+...}$.

allNodeData.name: Composition VS Sequence
allNodeData.description: Consider a coin tossed 4 times in a row. One could compute the probability of getting a specific sequence $HTHH$, but combinatorics is the study of $compositions$, in which we investigate the probability of getting 3 $H$'s and 1 $T$ in $any$ order.

allNodeData.name: Permutations
allNodeData.description:
For a sequence of $N$ $distinguishable$ objects, the number of different permutations of $W$ can be expressed in factoprial notation $N!$. That means, for any specific sequence, the probability is $\frac{1}{N!}$.

	If $instead$ there are elements which are $indistinguishable$, then $\frac{1}{N!}$ overcounts the possible $distinguishable$ sequences by a factor of $N_A!$ (The number of permutations of the indistinguishable elements) where $N_A$ is the number of indistinguishable elements $A$. Therefore the number of $distinguishable$ sequences is $\frac{N!}{N_A!}$.

	The general equation that accounts for multiple $distinguishable$ elements is:

	$W = \frac{N!}{n_i!n_j!n_k!...}$. This accounts for distinguishability of all degenerate elements.

	If there are only $2$ categories (success/failure, heads/tails etc.), The number of successes with $n$ successes out of $N$ trials is:

	$W(n,N) = \begin{pmatrix}N\\n\end{pmatrix}=\frac{N!}{n!(N-n)!}$

allNodeData.name: Probability Distribution Functions
allNodeData.description: A function which has property $\sum\limits_{i=1}^n p_i=1$ and describes the probability of different outcomes $p_i$. If the distribution is continuous then over $[a,b]$, then the summation becomes $1=\int_a^b rho(x)dx$ where $rho(x)$ is the probability density.

allNodeData.name: Binomial Distribution
allNodeData.description:
$P(n,N)=p^n(1-p)^{N-n}\frac{N!}{n!(N-n)!}$

This gives the probability of $n$ A outcomes and $N-n$ B outcomes irrepective of their sequence. The fraction gives coefficients for Pascal's Triangle which forms the coefficients of the expansion of $(x+y)^N$.

allNodeData.name: $n^{th} \ moments$
allNodeData.description:
The $n^{th}$ moment of a probability distribution function $p(x)$ is:

$\braket{x^n} = \int_a^b x^n p(x)dx = \frac{int_a^b x^n g(x)dx}{\int_a^b g(x)dx}$

Zeroth moment always gives 1, the first moment is the average or expectation value $\braket{x}$ The mean of a function is decribed by:

$\braket{f(x)} = \int_a^b f(x)p(x)dx = \frac{\int_a^b f(x)g(x)dx}{\int_a^b g(x)dx}$

allNodeData.name: Variance
allNodeData.description:
The variance $\sigma^2$ is a measure of the width of a distribution.

$\sigma^2 = \braket{(x-a)^2} = \braket{x^2- 2ax + a^2} = \braket{x^2}-\braket{x}^2 $ where $a=\braket{x}$

allNodeData.name: Maximization of Multiplicity
allNodeData.description: Systems tend towards states which have the greatest multiplicity in their configurations. That is, where $\frac{dW}{dn}=0$. For example: If you flipped a coin 4 times, there are many more possible sequences which contain 2 heads and 2 tails than 4 heads, therefore the most probably outcome is the former.

allNodeData.name: First law of Thermodynamics
allNodeData.description:
The internal energy $\Delta U$ changes when a system takes up or gives off heat $q$ or work $w$:

 $\Delta U = q + w$

This is a statement of the equivalence of heat and work. The internal energy is conserved; if $\Delta U$ increases in the system, the energy decreases in the surroundings.

allNodeData.name: Kinetic Theory of Gases
allNodeData.description:
Built upon the three novel concepts:

(1) Matter is composed of molecules that are not located at fixed positions in space, but are free to move through a space that is otherwise empty.

(2) Heat is the exchange of energy that takes place owing to the motions and collisions of molecules. In the kinetic theory, molecules collide and exchange energy like Newtonian billiard balls.

(3) Electromagnetic radiation can influence the motions of molecules. This is the basis for radiant heat.

Predicts:

$\frac{3}{2}kT = \frac{m\braket{v^2}}{2}$

allNodeData.name: The Second Law of Thermodynamics
allNodeData.description: Systems tend toward maximum multiplicity. For the case of energy, this means energy will flow in the direction that maximizes the multiplicity of the entire system.

allNodeData.name: Extrema of Constrained Functions
allNodeData.description:
We still have that:

$df = (\frac{\partial f}{\partial x})_y dx + (\frac{\partial f}{\partial y})_x dy = 0$

But we now also have a constraint function $g(x,y)$. Use the constraint to put $dx$ and $dy$ in terms of eachother, plug into $df$ and solve for the critical point.

allNodeData.name: Method of Lagrange Multipliers
allNodeData.description:
We imagine 2 level curves $l_f$ and $l_g$ where the functions $f(x,y)$ and $g(x,y)$ intersect. We are looking for places where $df=dg=0$, that is:

$df = (\frac{\partial f}{\partial x})_y dx + (\frac{\partial f}{\partial y})_x dy = 0$

$dg = (\frac{\partial g}{\partial x})_y dx + (\frac{\partial g}{\partial y})_x dy = 0$

	solving for $\frac{dy}{dx}$ gives:

$-\frac{\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}}{\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}} = \frac{dy}{dx}$

$-\frac{\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}}{\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}} = \frac{dy}{dx}$
	
such that:

$\frac{dy}{dx} = -\frac{\frac{\partial f}{\partial x}}{\frac{\partial f}{\partial y}} = -\frac{\frac{\partial g}{\partial x}}{\frac{\partial g}{\partial y}}$

This equation tells us that the ratio of the partial derivatives of each function w.r.t. $x$ and $y$ must be equal, that is:

$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x} = \lambda \frac{\partial g}{\partial x}$

$\frac{\partial f}{\partial y} = \lambda \frac{\partial g}{\partial y}$

For some $Lagrange$ $multiplier$ $\lambda$

The values $(x^*,y^*)$ that satisfy these equations are the extremum.

In general, for the extremum of $f(x_1,x_2,...,x_t)$ subject to more than one constraint, $g=c_1$, $h=c_2$, the lagrange multiplier method gives solutions:

$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_1}-\lambda \frac{\partial g}{\partial x_1} -\beta \frac{\partial h}{\partial x_1}-...=0$

$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_2}-\lambda \frac{\partial g}{\partial x_2} -\beta \frac{\partial h}{\partial x_2}-...=0$

$\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_t}-\lambda \frac{\partial g}{\partial x_t} -\beta \frac{\partial h}{\partial x_t}-...=0$

etc. where $\lambda$, $beta$, ... are the Lagrange multipliers for each constraint.
